HFT is a (relatively) new concept where computers do all the trading instead of humans. Many of them are located within blocks of stock exchanges because the speed of light becomes a limiting factor in how fast they can execute trades. The basic idea is that when a large mutual fund sells a lot of stock, the price will dip for a bit before returning to slightly lower than its normal level. 30 years ago, this would be over the course of 5-10 minutes. Now computers will capitalize on this by buying it as soon as possible then selling it a few seconds later. It helps smooth out "bumps" and reduce volatility of high-liquidity stocks, though there are arguments it can increase volatility of lower-liquidity/smaller stocks.

There are other algorithms, and HFTs hire very intelligent people to try to come up new algorithms to "beat the market" using computers. As other companies copy them, those algorithms become less effective, so it's a constant battle of new ideas as well as trying to improve the physical connections to get their trades in faster than other firms doing the same.

In 2008-2010, HFTs were extremely successful and represented a huge percentage of the trading on global markets. As the regulations have tightened and competition has increased, they've become less profitable, but they're still a force in the market.

This particular company used some algorithms that manipulated the market illegally. ZeroHedge appears to be a conspiracy theory website masquerading as business news that decided because one firm did some shady things that all HFTs are evil.
